article_title: Digital Fluency: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway
citation: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway: Digital Fluency. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Cybersecurity fluency proposed as a sixth component of digital fluency
description: Drawing on its cybersecurity pathway work, the article proposes adding cybersecurity fluency to the five-component framework. It states: "Based on our rapidly scaling work at Digital Promise's Center for Learner Pathway Innovations in designing, implementing, and supporting credentialed cybersecurity pathways nationwide, we would add a sixth component: cybersecurity fluency." It holds that every worker is on the frontline of keeping information and systems secure.
requirements: Understanding cybersecurity risks and employing proactive measures to protect data and access
target_learners: all workers in career pathways, whether or not security is officially part of their job
target_learning_goals: protecting data and access; managing cybersecurity risks
examples: Examples include managing securing point-of-sale systems from ransomware and protecting patient HIPAA data and medical IoT devices
key_sources: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway: Digital Fluency. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/2574439a-3a90-422d-80b6-d31caa93636b

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Children and Youth Behavioral Health Initiative (CYBHI)
description: The CYBHI, adopted in California's 2021/22 budget, aims to transform children and youth behavioral health into an upstream-focused ecosystem in which all children and youth are routinely screened, supported, and served. "Approximately $4 billion has been allocated over 5 years; funding grants are one-time and will be spent over 5 years, from 2022 through 2026." It has four focus areas: expanding equitable access with no wrong door, building prevention and treatment capacity, raising awareness, and delivering evidence-based care. Services target Californians aged birth through 25 via commercial plans and Medi-Cal, including a 24/7 virtual platform.
requirements: Partnerships across CalHHS and outside agencies, including K–12 and higher education systems
constraints: The guide notes the CYBHI does not provide immediate resources for direct services; it focuses on infrastructure
target_learning_goals: Behavioral health screening, support, and service access that enables children and youth to learn and thrive
examples: Components connected to student mental health include incentive grants to Medi-Cal managed care plans to partner with LEAs, funding for school-based counselors and coaches, and a virtual access platform
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Generative AI Feedback, English Writing and Teacher Rubrics: A Multiple-Case Study of CyberScholar
citation: Raigul Zheldibayeva, Ana Karina de Oliveira Nascimento, Vania Castro, Bill Cope and Mary Kalantzis. (2025). Generative AI Feedback, English Writing and Teacher Rubrics: A Multiple-Case Study of CyberScholar.
title: CyberScholar: a rubric-aligned GenAI writing-feedback platform using RAG, rubric agents, and a curated knowledge base
description: CyberScholar is a multimodal, multilingual writing workspace for Grade 4 and above in which students draft in a vertically divided editor with AI and human dialogue tools on the right. Its workflow includes CyberHelper for drafting assistance, CyberReviewer, which "delivers quantitative feedback with qualitative narrative justification from AI rubric agents, peers, teachers, or self-reflection," a Composition Report analyzing AI use via logfile data, teacher-built Rubric Agents using multiple-pass prompt engineering, and a Knowledge Base of "curated, educator-validated domain content stored in a vector database for retrieval -augmented generation." Foundation models are selectable, with student identities separated via the platform's API.
requirements: Teacher-provided rubrics, materials, and exemplars must be added to the knowledge base so feedback aligns with teacher expectations and the rubric
Teachers construct and calibrate rubric agents through onboarding
constraints: Bias-flagging and hallucination filters and restrictions on data retention and model training were adopted despite potential trade-offs in model flexibility and scoring stability
target_learners: K-12 students in grades 7-11 in the study (platform designed for Grade 4 and above)
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary writing development in ELA, Social Studies, and History with formative feedback aligned to teacher rubrics
examples: Piloted across five U.S. schools (four high schools, one rural middle school) during one semester, with students drafting, requesting rubric-aligned AI feedback, revising, and resubmitting
key_sources: Raigul Zheldibayeva, Ana Karina de Oliveira Nascimento, Vania Castro, Bill Cope and Mary Kalantzis. (2025). Generative AI Feedback, English Writing and Teacher Rubrics: A Multiple-Case Study of CyberScholar. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17055

article_title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
citation: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965
title: CyberAGENTS four-agent learning loop: Challenge, Buddy, Critic, and Reward agents
description: CyberAGENTS decomposes the gamified learning loop into four specialized agents coordinated by a central orchestrator. The article states "the framework decomposes gameplay into four specialized agents: ChallengeAgent,BuddyAgent,CriticAgent, andRewardAgent," enacting the cycle of challenge, learner attempt, evaluation, and progression. Each agent maps to a gamified learning function: progressive challenges, adaptive support, structured feedback, and mastery-based progression, with the RewardAgent assigning XP across tiers from Apprentice to Legendary.
requirements: A custom orchestrator-worker framework coordinating the four agents and maintaining shared gameplay state
LLM inference for agent reasoning and response generation
constraints: Sessions were configured at a novice difficulty level and designed to take approximately 5-15 minutes
target_learning_goals: Progressive challenge completion with adaptive support and mastery-based reward progression
examples: Table 1 maps ChallengeAgent to Progressive Challenges, BuddyAgent to Adaptive Support, CriticAgent to Structured Feedback, and RewardAgent to Mastery-Based Progression
key_sources: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965

article_title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
citation: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965
title: Competency-mapping module organizing curriculum topics by difficulty, prerequisites, and concept clusters
description: The competency-mapping module extracts structured competencies from course materials using a cybersecurity-specific competency schema. The extractor "identifies key entities such as tools, techniques, concepts, attacks, vulnerabilities, and defenses; assigns difficulty levels from Beginner to Expert; and maps instructional relations relevant to gameplay design, including prerequisites, concept clusters, and learning enablers." The resulting competency graph serves as the initialization blueprint for challenge generation, keeping gameplay curriculum-aligned from the outset.
requirements: Course materials from which structured competencies are extracted
A cybersecurity-specific competency schema with difficulty levels and instructional relations
constraints: Designed for cybersecurity curriculum materials; the article frames conceptual dependency management as especially important in this domain
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned challenge progression that avoids cognitive overload or fragmented learning
examples: The competency map encodes entries such as a Man-in-the-Middle attack with difficulty_level 3, exploits_vulnerabilities weak_encryption, and requires_tools Wireshark
key_sources: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Cyclical self-regulation feedback model for feedback engagement in a GenAI context
description: Adapting Zimmerman's cyclical self-regulated learning model, the paper proposes a cyclical self-regulation feedback model (Figure 2) with three phases: feedback forethought (setting feedback goals and planning based on understanding of GenAI's capabilities and limitations), feedback control (self-observation and self-monitoring of prompts and GenAI responses, refining interactions), and feedback retrospect (reflecting on feedback effectiveness and developing ethical awareness). 'This cyclical process ensures that feedback generated from GenAI is iterative and progressive, fostering continuous engagement and development.' The phases are interwoven with the eliciting, processing and enacting stages.
requirements: Students exercise agency to adapt to the new feedback environment; teachers assist with goal definition and model metacognitive strategies
constraints: The paper states that because GenAI application in feedback practices is still at an early stage, 'any current conceptualisations should remain provisional as GenAI evolves'
target_learning_goals: self-regulating feedback processes and enhancing feedback literacy
examples: Educators and researchers can use the model to identify primary challenges at each stage and design interventions facilitating adaptation to the GenAI feedback environment
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement
citation: Prast, E. J., Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Luit, J. E. H. (2018). Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement. Learning and Instruction, 54, 22-34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.009
title: The cycle of differentiation: a five-step expert-consensus model for differentiating primary mathematics instruction
description: The cycle of differentiation is the GROW project's expert-consensus model of what teachers should do to implement differentiation in daily mathematics practice. It comprises five steps: identification of educational needs (including diagnostic interviews and analysis of daily work), setting differentiated goals that are challenging but realistic, differentiated instruction (broad whole-class instruction, tailored subgroup instruction, individual adaptations), differentiated practice (quantitatively and qualitatively, including compacting and enriching material for high achievers), and evaluation of progress and process, which feeds back into needs identification. Students work in flexible within-class achievement groups part of the time and can switch groups as needs change.
requirements: Teachers need extensive subject matter knowledge as well as advanced diagnostic, didactical, pedagogical, and classroom management skills
Ongoing refined diagnostic measures beyond achievement tests to determine qualitative educational needs
Flexible within-class grouping so students can switch groups based on changes in educational needs
constraints: The article states the cycle represents best practice recommended by experts based on experiential knowledge, and quantitative empirical evidence proving differentiation has positive effects was scarce at the time of design
target_learners: Primary school students in grades 1-6 of diverse achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Meeting diverse educational needs in primary mathematics
examples: The PD programme taught teachers the cycle of differentiation and strategies for each step over ten three-hour team meetings spread across the schoolyear
key_sources: Prast, E. J., Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Luit, J. E. H. (2018). Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement. Learning and Instruction, 54, 22-34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.009

article_title: Supplemental Material for Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests
citation: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: CytonRK: a custom head-mounted portable EEG recorder for classroom use
description: The CytonRK is a bespoke head-mounted EEG device built by the lead author because no commercial device met classroom requirements. It uses an OPENBCI Cyton board with an ADS1299 8-channel converter, records at 250Hz to local micro-SD memory with a battery-backed real-time clock, and uses dry Silver Chloride comb electrodes on a 25mm elasticized harness designed for minimal invasiveness in hair.
requirements: Local memory recording was chosen because Bluetooth pairing of up to 26 devices in one classroom was impractical and school WiFi networks were infeasible
constraints: The article notes temporal electrode placement was moved from just in front to just behind the ears after participant feedback about pressure irritation
target_learners: high school students in naturalistic classroom settings
target_learning_goals: recording EEG-based indicators of attention and working memory during real classroom assessments
examples: Neurometric validation in UNSW's Future Minds Lab showed 12Hz flicker responses at O1/O2 and eyes-closed alpha peaks at parietal electrodes
key_sources: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. article_title: Optimists’ Creed: Brave New Cyberlearning, Evolving Utopias (Circa 2041)
citation: Winslow Burleson & Armanda Lewis. (2016). Optimists' Creed: Brave New Cyberlearning, Evolving Utopias (Circa 2041). Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:796–808. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0096-x
title: Four primary qualities of cyberlearning environments: rich stories, open streaming content, shared contribution, and re-solvable challenges
description: The article enumerates the primary qualities of its envisioned cyberlearning environments: personal stories and interactive experiences that 'make it rich'; open streaming content that 'make it real and compelling'; contributions that 'make it yours, together'; and wicked challenges that can be iteratively 're-solved'. Each quality pairs an experiential feature with a learning function—dreams and storytelling for ethical understanding, multimodal simulation for visceral understanding of implications, active ownership of learning trajectories for expertise and collaboration, and iterative re-solving for societal progress.
requirements: Embedded cyberlearning phenomena, real-world and open-world data sources, and empowered learners, peer tutors, and mentors
target_learners: learners, peer tutors, and mentors of all ages and stages
examples: Open streaming content examples include flying drones over Antarctica and obtaining data from LEGO robots on the moon and instruments on Mars
key_sources: Winslow Burleson & Armanda Lewis. (2016). Optimists' Creed: Brave New Cyberlearning, Evolving Utopias (Circa 2041). Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:796–808. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0096-x

article_title: Self-regulated learning in the clinical context: a systematic review.
citation: van Houten‐Schat Maaike A, Berkhout Joris J, van Dijk Nynke, Endedijk Maaike D, Jaarsma A Debbie, Diemers Agnes D. (2018). Self‐regulated learning in the clinical context: a systematic review. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13615
title: Cyclical three-phase SRL models (Zimmerman, Knowles, Pintrich) frame SRL as goal setting, plan implementation and self-evaluation, but stem from classroom research
description: The review reports that included studies used the cyclical three-phase model of Zimmerman, the theoretical model of Knowles, or a framework based on Pintrich's principles. These theories "agree upon active engagement, goal setting, implementation of a plan and self‐evaluation of the process". The review also cites Sitzmann and Ely's categorisation of SRL processes into regulatory agent (goal setting), regulatory mechanism (planning, monitoring, strategies, motivation, emotion control) and regulatory appraisal (self-evaluation, attributions, self-efficacy). The authors caution these classroom-derived models cannot easily be applied to the complex clinical context.
requirements: A theoretical framework is needed to study SRL, though the review found one is often lacking in clinical-context studies
constraints: The review states these frameworks stemmed from classroom-setting research and, given the known influence of context on SRL, cannot be applied easily to the complex clinical context
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning in the clinical workplace
key_sources: van Houten‐Schat Maaike A, Berkhout Joris J, van Dijk Nynke, Endedijk Maaike D, Jaarsma A Debbie, Diemers Agnes D. (2018). Self‐regulated learning in the clinical context: a systematic review. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13615

article_title: Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course
citation: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166
title: Cyclic model of computer modeling stages culminating in computing experiment
description: The article presents computer modeling as a sequence of stages shown in a flowchart (Figure 1), from structural analysis of the object through model construction to computing experiment. It states "The modeling method is cycling in character", so that for each concretized model all methodology steps are repeated, with the computing stage recurring checks and calculations for different model parameters. The stages serve one purpose: an adequate quantitative description of the studied phenomenon with necessary accuracy for minimal machine time.
requirements: Each stage is interconnected with the others while retaining its own specifics
constraints: The article notes modeling is "the most modern and not quite developed training method"
target_learners: secondary school pupils in computer science courses
target_learning_goals: understanding of modeling methodology and computing experiment
examples: The article illustrates the first stage, structural analysis of the object, with tasks such as determining tarpaulin needed for tent production and calculating a train's speed from wheel knocks
key_sources: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166

article_title: Effects of Blackboard's Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students
citation: Alharbi, M. (2015). Effects of Blackboard’s Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n6p111
title: A cyclical integrated reading/writing learning cycle using discussion boards, blogs and wikis
description: The article describes a recurring instructional cycle in which the tutor introduces reading/writing topics, assigns cooperative online work teams, and guides students through engagement in reading, discussion-board responses, personal blogging, and collaborative wiki construction. Each course unit takes three classes plus homework per week, with teams' wikis made public for inter-team reading, feedback and editing. The cycle is cyclical and continues with each course unit until the end of the semester.
requirements: A tutor-monitored process with wiki evaluation rubrics to help inter-team members provide and assess feedback on students' writings
constraints: Inter-team work is permitted only on wiki proofreading, editing and revising
examples: The instructor and learners designed forum, blog and wiki module content collaboratively, choosing tasks, assigning roles, finding resource links, providing tutor support, and incorporating evaluation rubrics
key_sources: Alharbi, M. (2015). Effects of Blackboard’s Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n6p111
